questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a BP of 156/96 mmHg at a routine review and 152/94 mmHg on repeat. He has no symptoms. He smokes, has a BMI of 32 kg/m² and adds salt to his food. Ambulatory monitoring shows a daytime average of 148/92 mmHg. His potassium, creatinine and urinalysis are normal and there are no bruits.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Older, asymptomatic, obese smoker with a salty diet, normal bloods and no red flags: essential hypertension, which is 90 to 95% of cases.

clues: potassium, creatinine and urinalysis are normal
steps.x: Older age, risk factors (obesity, salt, smoking), no symptoms and normal tests: **no red flags** for a secondary cause.

elim: Presents young, with radio-femoral delay; he is 64 with normal pulses implied.
Gives episodic headache, sweating and palpitations; he is asymptomatic.
Usually low potassium; his potassium is normal.
Expect a bruit, resistant hypertension or flash pulmonary oedema; none here.

steps.x: **B. Essential hypertension.** Essential hypertension is the default when there are no red flags (90 to 95% of cases).

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl with short stature and a webbed neck is seen in clinic. Her BP is 162/94 mmHg in the right arm. Her femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with her radial pulses, and there is a systolic murmur heard over her back. Her potassium and creatinine are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
questions.e: Radio-femoral delay, weak femorals and a murmur over the back in a girl with Turner features is coarctation of the aorta, a secondary cause to suspect in anyone under 40.

clues: short stature and a webbed neck
femoral pulses are weak and delayed
steps.x: Young (<40) plus Turner features plus **radio-femoral delay**: a structural secondary cause.

elim: Unlikely at 16 with a structural sign (radio-femoral delay).
Episodic adrenergic symptoms, not delayed femoral pulses.
Hypokalaemia expected; potassium is normal.
Gives an abdominal bruit, not radio-femoral delay or a murmur over the back.

steps.x: **A. Coarctation of the aorta.** Young + radio-femoral delay = coarctation; Turner syndrome is the classic association.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has had three admissions in a year with sudden severe breathlessness, each time with pulmonary oedema on chest X-ray. Echocardiograms between episodes show normal left ventricular function. His BP is 176/98 mmHg despite amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide. He smokes and has claudication. A bruit is heard to the left of the umbilicus.

visual.title: Where the bruit is
visual.caption: A para-umbilical bruit points to renal artery stenosis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.e: Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with normal LV function, an abdominal bruit and resistance to three agents in an arteriopath is atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.

clues: three admissions in a year with sudden severe breathlessness
bruit is heard to the left of the umbilicus
steps.x: Flash pulmonary oedema + normal LV + abdominal bruit + resistant to 3 drugs in a vasculopath.

elim: Would show central obesity, striae and proximal myopathy.
Does not explain flash oedema, an abdominal bruit and resistance to three drugs.
Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; none described.
Hypokalaemia and fatigue; no bruit or flash oedema.

steps.x: **E. Renal artery stenosis.** Resistant hypertension + flash pulmonary oedema + bruit = renal artery stenosis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has a BP of 166/102 mmHg, confirmed on ambulatory monitoring. She takes no medication. She has felt lethargic with headaches and muscle weakness for months. She has no episodes of sweating or palpitations.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia and high-normal sodium, lethargy and weakness, on no diuretic, is primary hyperaldosteronism.

clues: lethargic with headaches and muscle weakness
steps.x: Unprovoked **low potassium** with high-normal sodium in a hypertensive patient on no diuretics.

elim: Can lower potassium but she has no cushingoid features; isolated hypokalaemia and hypernatraemia fit Conn's.
Does not cause spontaneous hypokalaemia in an untreated patient.
Episodic triad is absent and potassium is not typically low.
No bruit or flash oedema, and she is young without vascular disease.

steps.x: **D. Primary hyperaldosteronism.** Hypertension + low K+ (not on diuretics) = think primary hyperaldosteronism first.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has hypertension and a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L. His plasma aldosterone:renin ratio is markedly raised. High-resolution CT of the abdomen shows normal-looking adrenal glands. Adrenal venous sampling shows equally high aldosterone from both adrenal veins.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hyperaldosteronism?
questions.e: Bilateral, equal aldosterone secretion with normal CT is bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia, the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism; it is treated with spironolactone.

clues: equally high aldosterone from both adrenal veins
steps.x: Raised ratio = primary (renin suppressed). **Both** sides secreting with normal CT = bilateral disease.

elim: Rare, and would show a large mass on CT.
Gives a unilateral source on sampling, often with a nodule on CT.
Causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with high renin, so the ratio would not be raised.
Renin would be high, so the aldosterone:renin ratio would be normal or low.

steps.x: **C. Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia.** Commonest cause of Conn's is bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia (medical treatment), not an adenoma.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has had episodes of pounding headache, drenching sweats and palpitations lasting 20 minutes for 2 months. He has many soft skin nodules and several café-au-lait macules. During an episode his pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 212/118 mmHg; between episodes it is 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Paroxysms of headache, sweating and tachycardia with BP surges in a man with neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules (NF1) is phaeochromocytoma.

clues: pounding headache, drenching sweats and palpitations
soft skin nodules and several café-au-lait macules
steps.x: Classic triad, **episodic**, and **NF1** skin signs.

elim: Causes flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze, and is not linked with neurofibromatosis.
Symptoms are continuous, not 20-minute paroxysms with BP surges.
Does not cause BP of 212/118 mmHg, and his skin signs point to NF1.
Sustained hypertension with low potassium, not paroxysms.

steps.x: **D. Phaeochromocytoma.** Episodic headache + sweating + tachycardia, especially with NF1, MEN2 or VHL = phaeochromocytoma.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has had a phaeochromocytoma confirmed on plasma free metanephrines and CT. Her mother had a thyroidectomy for a thyroid cancer in her thirties. Genetic testing shows a RET proto-oncogene mutation. She is referred for further screening.
questions.q: Which other tumour is she most at risk of?
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma with a RET mutation is MEN2, which carries medullary thyroid carcinoma (from calcitonin-secreting C cells).

steps.x: Phaeo + family thyroid cancer + **RET** = MEN2.

elim: Occurs in the elderly and is not part of MEN2.
Part of MEN1 (pancreatic tumours), not MEN2.
Commonest thyroid cancer but not associated with RET-driven MEN2.
Part of MEN1, not MEN2.

steps.x: **C. Medullary thyroid carcinoma.** MEN2 = phaeochromocytoma + medullary thyroid carcinoma (± hyperparathyroidism in 2A).

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has a BP of 164/100 mmHg. Over a year she has gained weight around her abdomen, bruises easily and struggles to rise from a chair. She has wide purple striae on her abdomen. Her fasting glucose is 7.4 mmol/L and potassium 3.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
questions.e: Central obesity, wide purple striae, easy bruising, proximal myopathy and hyperglycaemia with hypertension is Cushing's syndrome, an endocrine cause of secondary hypertension.

clues: struggles to rise from a chair
steps.x: Cushingoid features (central obesity, **purple striae**, bruising, **proximal myopathy**) in a young hypertensive woman.

elim: Causes weight gain but not purple striae, bruising or hyperglycaemia.
Gives episodic adrenergic symptoms and weight loss, not central obesity.
Causes weight gain and hirsutism but not proximal myopathy, bruising and purple striae.
Low potassium and hypertension but no cushingoid habitus.

steps.x: **A. Cushing's syndrome.** Hypertension + cushingoid features = Cushing's syndrome, an endocrine secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 54 year old lorry driver has hypertension that remains above target on three drugs. His wife says he snores loudly and stops breathing at night. He wakes with headaches and falls asleep while watching TV. His BMI is 39 kg/m² and collar size 19 inches. His potassium and cortisol are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.e: Resistant hypertension with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness and a thick neck is obstructive sleep apnoea.

clues: snores loudly and stops breathing at night
steps.x: Witnessed apnoeas + daytime sleepiness + obesity + **resistant** hypertension.

elim: His cortisol is normal and there are no striae or myopathy.
Can cause sleepiness, but witnessed apnoeas and snoring point to OSA.
Gives episodic sweating and palpitations, not snoring and apnoeas.
A cause of resistant hypertension, but his potassium is normal.

steps.x: **C. Obstructive sleep apnoea.** Always ask about snoring and sleepiness in resistant hypertension: OSA is a common secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone 15 mg daily for 5 months. Her BP was 124/78 mmHg before treatment and is now 158/96 mmHg on two readings, with ambulatory monitoring confirming hypertension. Her potassium is 3.8 mmol/L and creatinine normal. There are no bruits.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
questions.e: New hypertension after starting long-term prednisolone, with a normal BP before, is drug-induced (steroid) secondary hypertension.

steps.x: Normal BP **before** the steroid, raised after: a drug cause.

elim: Her BP was normal until the steroid was started; a drug cause must be considered first.
No snoring, apnoeas or sleepiness described.
Potassium is normal and the timing fits the drug.
No bruit, flash oedema or resistance to treatment.

steps.x: **C. Prednisolone therapy.** Check the drug history: steroids and the combined pill are common secondary causes.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has 3 days of headache, vomiting and blurred vision. He stopped his tablets months ago. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 238/136 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling with flame haemorrhages. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and protein 3+.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: BP above 180/120 mmHg with papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages and AKI is malignant (accelerated) hypertension, a hypertensive emergency.

clues: bilateral optic disc swelling with flame haemorrhages
steps.x: Very high BP + **papilloedema** + **AKI** (blood, protein, high creatinine) = acute end-organ damage.

elim: Causes papilloedema but not BP of 238/136 mmHg with AKI.
Does not cause papilloedema, AKI or severe hypertension.
Thunderclap onset over seconds, not 3 days, and does not cause AKI.
Is a clinic-only rise without end-organ damage.

steps.x: **B. Malignant hypertension.** Severe hypertension + papilloedema or AKI = malignant hypertension: admit for controlled IV treatment.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for 20 years. He has become breathless on exertion. His BP is 172/96 mmHg and there is a forceful, non-displaced apex beat. His ECG shows tall QRS voltages in the chest leads with lateral T-wave inversion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
o: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion
Dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesia
questions.e: Chronic pressure overload from uncontrolled hypertension causes concentric LVH (heaving, non-displaced apex, high ECG voltages), which leads to heart failure.

steps.x: Long-standing pressure load + heaving apex + voltage criteria = **LVH**.

elim: This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a genetic disease, not hypertensive heart disease.
Dilated cardiomyopathy; the apex would be displaced.
Gives small complexes on ECG, not tall voltages.
From pulmonary hypertension or PE, not systemic hypertension.

steps.x: **B. Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy.** Hypertension's cardiac end-organ damage is concentric LVH, progressing to heart failure.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension suddenly develops left-sided weakness and headache. Her BP is 204/108 mmHg. CT head shows an acute haemorrhage in the right basal ganglia. She has no history of trauma and takes no anticoagulants.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of the haemorrhage?
questions.e: Sustained hypertension damages small penetrating arteries (arteriolosclerosis) through mechanical stress, causing deep basal ganglia haemorrhage and stroke.

steps.x: Deep (basal ganglia) bleed in an older patient with years of uncontrolled BP.

elim: Presents younger, often with seizures; deep haemorrhage in an older hypertensive is hypertensive.
Causes subarachnoid blood, not a deep basal ganglia bleed.
Rare; usually small bleeds in younger patients.
Causes lobar (cortical) bleeds, not deep basal ganglia bleeds.

steps.x: **E. Chronic hypertension.** Deep intracerebral haemorrhage = hypertensive small-vessel damage; lobar bleed = amyloid.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a BP of 174/108 mmHg at a work health check, confirmed by ambulatory monitoring. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, has a BMI of 28 kg/m², eats takeaways most nights and his father had hypertension in his sixties. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests he should be investigated for a secondary cause?
o: Father had hypertension in his sixties
questions.e: Hypertension under 40, especially when severe, should prompt a search for a secondary cause; the other features are ordinary risk factors for essential hypertension.

clues: father had hypertension in his sixties
steps.x: Red flags for a secondary cause: **young (<40)**, severe, sudden onset, resistant, or specific signs.

elim: Overweight is a risk factor for essential hypertension, not a red flag.
A family history supports essential (genetic) hypertension.
Salt is an environmental risk factor for essential hypertension.
A cardiovascular risk factor, not a pointer to a secondary cause.

steps.x: **A. Age under 40 years.** Under 40 with hypertension = look for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a BP of 164/102 mmHg. He has had two episodes of visible haematuria and dull loin pain. His father started dialysis at 50. On examination both flanks have large, irregular ballotable masses. His creatinine is 148 µmol/L.

visual.title: Where the masses are
visual.caption: Bilateral ballotable flank masses: enlarged polycystic kidneys.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.e: Bilateral ballotable kidneys, haematuria, CKD and a parent on dialysis is ADPKD, a renal (CKD) cause of secondary hypertension.

clues: both flanks have large, irregular ballotable masses
steps.x: A specific finding pointing to a cause: bilateral **renal masses** + family history.

elim: Would cause radio-femoral delay, not flank masses or haematuria.
Does not explain bilateral renal masses, haematuria and a family history of dialysis.
Adrenal tumour with episodic symptoms; not bilateral renal masses.
Usually a single mass; bilateral irregular kidneys with a family history fit ADPKD.

steps.x: **A. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.** CKD is a common renal cause of secondary hypertension; ADPKD is the inherited one.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has lost 6 kg in 2 months despite a good appetite. She feels hot, anxious and has a fine tremor. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 156/72 mmHg. She has lid lag and a smooth goitre. Her symptoms are continuous rather than episodic.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
questions.e: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, lid lag and a goitre with systolic hypertension is hyperthyroidism, an endocrine secondary cause.

clues: lid lag and a smooth goitre
steps.x: Continuous adrenergic features + **goitre** + lid lag = thyroid.

elim: Structural cause with radio-femoral delay; no weight loss or tremor.
Causes weight gain, not weight loss.
Symptoms are paroxysmal; hers are continuous with a goitre.
No weight loss, tremor or goitre; hypokalaemia instead.

steps.x: **C. Hyperthyroidism.** Thyroid disease is an endocrine cause of secondary hypertension; continuous symptoms separate it from phaeo.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a clinic BP of 154/96 mmHg and 150/94 mmHg on repeat. He is a night-shift worker and tried ambulatory monitoring but removed the cuff after 2 hours because it kept waking him. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Clinic BP above 140/90 mmHg must be confirmed out of clinic; ABPM is preferred, but HBPM (average above 135/85 mmHg) is the alternative when ABPM is not tolerated.

steps.x: Clinic BP >140/90 needs **out-of-clinic confirmation**; ABPM was not tolerated.

elim: Looks for LVH, but does not confirm the diagnosis of hypertension.
Screens for a secondary cause; the diagnosis is not yet confirmed.
Delays diagnosis; clinic readings alone can be white-coat.
Treatment before confirming with out-of-clinic readings risks treating white-coat hypertension.

steps.x: **B. Home blood pressure monitoring.** Confirm with ABPM; if not tolerated, use HBPM (threshold 135/85 mmHg).

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has a clinic BP of 168/104 mmHg. Ambulatory monitoring shows a daytime average of 154/97 mmHg. She has no symptoms, no headache or visual disturbance, and her urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate interpretation of these results?
questions.e: Clinic ≥160/100 mmHg with daytime ABPM ≥150/95 mmHg is stage 2 hypertension; stage 1 is clinic ≥140/90 and ABPM ≥135/85.

steps.x: Clinic ≥160/100 and ABPM ≥150/95: both reach **stage 2** thresholds.

elim: Needs severe BP (≥180/120 mmHg) with papilloedema or acute organ damage.
Daytime ABPM of 154/97 is well above 135/85 mmHg.
Stage 1 is ABPM ≥135/85 but below 150/95 mmHg.
ABPM is also raised, so the rise is not clinic-only.

steps.x: **D. Stage 2 hypertension.** Stage 1: 140/90 clinic, 135/85 ABPM. Stage 2: 160/100 clinic, 150/95 ABPM.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has newly confirmed hypertension with a daytime ambulatory average of 152/96 mmHg. He has no symptoms. His GP has sent blood for FBC, U&Es, lipids and HbA1c, and a urine sample for albumin:creatinine ratio and dipstick.
questions.q: Which additional investigation should be part of his routine baseline assessment?
questions.e: Baseline assessment of everyone with hypertension includes bloods (FBC, U&Es), urinalysis and a 12-lead ECG to look for LVH and other end-organ damage.

steps.x: Baseline work-up: FBC, U&Es, urinalysis and **ECG** for end-organ damage (LVH).

elim: Not a baseline test; reserved for specific structural questions.
Used for suspected angina, not routine hypertension work-up.
Not used in the assessment of hypertension.
Only if phaeochromocytoma is suspected; he has no red flags.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** Every new hypertensive: bloods, urine and a 12-lead ECG.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a clinic BP of 186/124 mmHg at a routine appointment, and 184/122 mmHg on repeat. She feels well, with no headache, chest pain, breathlessness or visual symptoms. She is alert and orientated with no focal neurological signs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Clinic BP ≥180/120 mmHg without worrying symptoms needs urgent tests for end-organ damage, including fundoscopy for papilloedema and haemorrhages and a urine dipstick.

steps.x: BP **≥180/120** = look for end-organ damage today (fundi, urine).

elim: At ≥180/120 mmHg, end-organ damage must be looked for now, not after weeks.
She has no neurological symptoms or signs.
No episodic symptoms; not the first test.
Not urgent and not the first test for severe hypertension.

steps.x: **C. Fundoscopy.** ≥180/120 mmHg: urgent fundoscopy and urine dipstick; papilloedema means same-day admission.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with von Hippel-Lindau disease, who had a retinal haemangioblastoma treated last year, has had attacks of palpitations, sweating and headache. His BP during an attack was 196/112 mmHg. His local laboratory does not offer plasma metanephrine testing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma is confirmed biochemically first: plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, then the tumour is localised by imaging.

clues: does not offer plasma metanephrine testing
steps.x: VHL + classic triad = phaeo. Plasma test unavailable, so use the **urinary** alternative.

elim: Used to lateralise aldosterone secretion in Conn's, not phaeochromocytoma.
Tumour localisation comes after biochemical confirmation.
A functional localisation scan used after biochemistry, not first.
Screens for primary hyperaldosteronism, not phaeochromocytoma.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines.** Biochemistry before imaging: plasma free (or 24 h urinary fractionated) metanephrines.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has hypertension resistant to three drugs and a potassium of 3.2 mmol/L. Her plasma aldosterone:renin ratio is raised, with suppressed renin. She has no cushingoid features or episodic symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: In primary hyperaldosteronism the order is aldosterone:renin ratio, then high-resolution CT of the adrenals, then adrenal venous sampling.

clues: ratio is raised, with suppressed renin
steps.x: Raised ratio with low renin = primary hyperaldosteronism confirmed biochemically; now **image**.

elim: Comes after CT, to lateralise secretion before surgery.
Cushing's disease work-up; she has no cushingoid features.
Screens for Cushing's, not hyperaldosteronism.
Screens for phaeochromocytoma; she has no episodic symptoms.

steps.x: **B. High-resolution CT of the abdomen.** Ratio → CT abdomen → adrenal venous sampling.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has primary hyperaldosteronism with a raised aldosterone:renin ratio and hypokalaemia. High-resolution CT shows a 9 mm nodule in the left adrenal gland and a normal right adrenal. He is fit and wishes to have surgery if it would cure him.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Before adrenalectomy, adrenal venous sampling shows whether aldosterone comes from the nodule side or from both glands, since small nodules are often non-functioning.

clues: 9 mm nodule in the left adrenal gland
steps.x: CT nodule does not prove it is the source; surgery needs **lateralisation**.

elim: Used for staging malignancy, not lateralising aldosterone secretion.
Localises phaeochromocytoma, not aldosterone-secreting tissue.
The pituitary is not involved in primary hyperaldosteronism.
Delays a decision; small nodules are often non-functioning incidentalomas.

steps.x: **A. Adrenal venous sampling.** Adrenal venous sampling is the last step before surgery for Conn's.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease started ramipril 2 weeks ago. His creatinine has risen from 102 to 168 µmol/L. His BP is 150/88 mmHg. Urinalysis is bland. The ramipril has been stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: A sharp creatinine rise after an ACE inhibitor in an arteriopath suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis, because ACEi removes the efferent arteriolar constriction that maintains GFR; confirm with renal imaging (MR or CT angiography).

steps.x: Creatinine jump of over 30% on ACEi in a vasculopath = suspect **renal artery stenosis**.

elim: Lateralises aldosterone secretion; not relevant to renovascular disease.
Images the coronary, not renal, arteries.
Tests for phaeochromocytoma; there are no paroxysms.
For glomerular disease with active urine; his urine is bland.

steps.x: **C. Magnetic resonance renal angiography.** Suspected secondary (renovascular) hypertension needs renal imaging such as MR angiography.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman of South Asian origin has stage 2 hypertension confirmed on ambulatory monitoring. She does not have diabetes or kidney disease. She is not pregnant and is using an IUS for contraception. Her U&Es are normal and her echocardiogram shows no aortic stenosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: Under 55 and not of Black African or Caribbean origin, first-line is an ACE inhibitor (check U&Es first; avoid in pregnancy and significant aortic stenosis). South Asian patients follow the non-Black pathway.

steps.x: Under 55, **not Black** (South Asian counts as non-Black), no contraindications.

elim: First-line only if aged 55 or over, or of Black African or Caribbean origin.
Beta-blockers are not first-line for hypertension without another indication.
An alpha-blocker kept for step 4.
Thiazide-like diuretics are step 3 (or step 2 if intolerant).

steps.x: **E. Ramipril.** Under 55 and not Black: ACE inhibitor first.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man of Black African origin has a daytime ambulatory average of 158/99 mmHg. He has no diabetes or kidney disease. His U&Es are normal. He has been following lifestyle advice for 3 months without improvement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: Patients of Black African or Caribbean origin start with a calcium channel blocker at any age; age under 55 does not change this.

steps.x: Black African origin = **CCB first** regardless of being under 55.

elim: Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
Step 4 option only.
ACEi/ARB are less effective first-line in Black patients without diabetes.
Step 4 for resistant hypertension with K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L.

steps.x: **A. Amlodipine.** ≥55 or Black African/Caribbean: calcium channel blocker first.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man of Black Caribbean origin has type 2 diabetes and newly confirmed hypertension with an ambulatory average of 150/94 mmHg. His urine albumin:creatinine ratio is raised and potassium is 4.3 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: Diabetes (or CKD) favours an ACE inhibitor or ARB regardless of age or ethnicity; in Black patients an ARB is preferred to an ACE inhibitor.

steps.x: Diabetes with albuminuria overrides age and ethnicity: **RAAS blockade**.

elim: His diabetes and albuminuria favour RAAS blockade over a CCB.
Not a first-line antihypertensive.
Step 4 option only.
Thiazide-like diuretics are later steps.

steps.x: **E. Losartan.** Diabetes or CKD: ACEi/ARB first whatever the age or ethnicity.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a clinic BP of 146/92 mmHg and a daytime ambulatory average of 139/87 mmHg. She has no diabetes, kidney disease or cardiovascular disease. Her ECG, urinalysis and fundi are normal. Her QRISK3 score is 4%.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Stage 1 hypertension (ABPM ≥135/85 but <150/95 mmHg) with no end-organ damage and low risk is managed with lifestyle advice: weight loss, salt under 6 g a day, exercise, less alcohol and no smoking.

clues: ECG, urinalysis and fundi are normal
steps.x: **Stage 1** on ABPM, low risk, no end-organ damage.

elim: Drug treatment is not needed for low-risk stage 1 hypertension.
Her QRISK3 is below 10%.
No end-organ damage, diabetes, CVD or high risk, so drugs are not indicated yet.
The diagnosis is already confirmed.

steps.x: **C. Lifestyle advice alone.** Low-risk stage 1: lifestyle advice alone (salt <6 g/day, weight, exercise, alcohol, smoking).

questions.stem: A 52 year old white man has taken ramipril 10 mg daily for 4 months. He takes it reliably. His clinic BP is now 152/94 mmHg on two readings. His potassium is 4.6 mmol/L and creatinine stable. He has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Above the clinic target of <140/90 mmHg on an ACE inhibitor, step 2 adds a calcium channel blocker (or a thiazide-like diuretic if a CCB is not tolerated).

steps.x: Adherent, maximal ACEi, still above **140/90**: step 2.

elim: Beta-blockers are only a step 4 option.
Alpha-blockers are step 4.
Combining an ACEi with an ARB is not recommended (hyperkalaemia, AKI).
Step 4, and his potassium is above 4.5 mmol/L.

steps.x: **A. Add amlodipine.** Step 2 = ACEi/ARB + CCB (thiazide-like if CCB not tolerated).

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has hypertension treated with amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg daily, both taken reliably. Her clinic BP is 156/92 mmHg and home readings average 148/88 mmHg. Her potassium is 4.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Step 3 after ACEi plus CCB is a thiazide-like diuretic, indapamide first and bendroflumethiazide second.

clues: amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg daily
steps.x: Already on ACEi + CCB = **step 3**.

elim: Beta-blockers belong to step 4.
A thiazide-like diuretic is right, but indapamide is preferred first.
Dual ACEi plus ARB blockade is not recommended.
Step 4, used only once a thiazide-like diuretic has been added.

steps.x: **C. Add indapamide.** Step 3 = add a thiazide-like diuretic: indapamide first.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has had confusion and a painful swollen big toe for a week. He takes amlodipine, ramipril and a third antihypertensive started 2 months ago.
questions.q: Which drug was most likely started 2 months ago?
questions.e: Thiazide-like diuretics cause hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia (with hypocalciuria), raised urate with gout, and erectile dysfunction.

clues: confusion and a painful swollen big toe
steps.x: Low Na, low K, **high Ca**, high urate and gout: the classic thiazide picture.

elim: Causes postural hypotension, not electrolyte changes or gout.
Tends to raise potassium and does not cause hyponatraemia with hypercalcaemia.
Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not electrolyte changes.
Raises potassium and causes gynaecomastia.

steps.x: **B. Indapamide.** Thiazide side effects: low Na, low K, high Ca, gout, erectile dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 62 year old white woman has a clinic BP of 166/102 mmHg and a daytime ambulatory average of 156/98 mmHg. She has no diabetes or kidney disease. Her QRISK3 score is 16%. She has tried to reduce salt and alcohol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Stage 2 hypertension aged over 55 with QRISK above 10%: offer amlodipine, lifestyle advice and atorvastatin, aiming for a clinic BP below 140/90 mmHg.

steps.x: **Stage 2**, age ≥55 (CCB), QRISK **>10%** (statin).

elim: Her QRISK3 above 10% means a statin should also be offered.
Stage 2 hypertension needs drug treatment.
She is 55 or over, so a CCB is first-line, not an ACEi.
Starting two antihypertensives at once skips the step 1 choice.

steps.x: **B. Amlodipine, atorvastatin and lifestyle advice.** Stage 2, over 55, QRISK >10%: amlodipine + atorvastatin + lifestyle.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with chronic hypertension controlled on lisinopril has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. Her BP is 136/86 mmHg. She does not have asthma. She asks what to do about her blood pressure tablet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are avoided in pregnancy; labetalol is first-line, with nifedipine (for example in asthma) or methyldopa as alternatives.

steps.x: Pregnant on an **ACEi**: stop it. No asthma, so a beta-blocker is fine.

elim: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and must be stopped in pregnancy.
ARBs are also contraindicated in pregnancy.
Diuretics are not recommended for hypertension in pregnancy.
Anti-androgenic; not used in pregnancy.

steps.x: **D. Stop lisinopril and start labetalol.** Pregnancy: labetalol first, then nifedipine or methyldopa; never ACEi/ARB.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has hypertension and heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction of 30%. He takes bisoprolol, ramipril, furosemide and spironolactone. His BP is 158/90 mmHg. He also has stable angina. His GP is considering adding another antihypertensive.
questions.q: Which drug should be avoided?
questions.e: Verapamil is negatively inotropic and can precipitate or worsen pulmonary oedema in chronic heart failure, and it should not be combined with a beta-blocker.

clues: heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction of 30%
steps.x: HFrEF + already on a **beta-blocker**: avoid rate-limiting CCBs.

elim: A dihydropyridine CCB that is safe in heart failure if extra BP control is needed.
Improves survival in HFrEF and is already prescribed.
Relieves congestion in heart failure.
Improves survival in HFrEF.

steps.x: **E. Verapamil.** Avoid verapamil in heart failure (pulmonary oedema).

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has severe headache and confusion. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 236/138 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema and his creatinine is 212 µmol/L (baseline 90). He has no asthma and has not used cocaine. A junior doctor suggests bringing his BP to normal within the hour.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV labetalol with gradual BP reduction
Oral amlodipine and review in 1 week
Sublingual nifedipine to normalise BP within the hour
questions.e: Malignant hypertension is treated with IV labetalol, lowering BP in a controlled way over hours, because a rapid drop causes ischaemia when autoregulation has reset.

steps.x: Papilloedema + AKI = **emergency** needing IV treatment, but not a rapid drop.

elim: Not a treatment for hypertensive emergency without fluid overload.
Too slow for acute end-organ damage.
Oral ACEi in AKI is unsafe and too slow.
Rapid falls cause cerebral, renal and coronary ischaemia.

steps.x: **B. IV labetalol with gradual BP reduction.** Malignant hypertension: IV labetalol, controlled reduction, never a sudden drop.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has resistant hypertension despite adherence to ramipril, amlodipine and indapamide. Her clinic BP is 158/96 mmHg, confirmed by ambulatory monitoring. Her potassium is 4.9 mmol/L. She has moderate asthma requiring a preventer inhaler.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: At step 4, potassium above 4.5 mmol/L means a beta-blocker or alpha-1 blocker rather than spironolactone; asthma rules out the beta-blocker, so doxazosin.

steps.x: Step 4 with **K+ >4.5** = beta- or alpha-blocker; **asthma** removes the beta-blocker.

elim: Beta-blockers are an option when K+ >4.5 mmol/L, but are contraindicated in asthma.
She is already on a thiazide-like diuretic.
Dual RAAS blockade would raise potassium further.
Her potassium is above 4.5 mmol/L, so it risks hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: **C. Add doxazosin.** Step 4: K+ ≤4.5 spironolactone; K+ >4.5 beta-blocker or alpha-blocker.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with resistant hypertension had a fourth drug added 3 months ago because his potassium was 3.9 mmol/L. His BP is now 134/82 mmHg. He has developed tender swelling under both nipples. His potassium is 5.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Spironolactone is the step 4 drug when K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L; as an aldosterone antagonist with anti-androgenic effects it causes hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia.

steps.x: Step 4 drug chosen for **K+ ≤4.5**, then gynaecomastia and **hyperkalaemia**.

elim: Causes ankle oedema and gum hypertrophy, not gynaecomastia.
Causes lethargy and erectile dysfunction, not gynaecomastia.
Causes postural hypotension.
Causes low, not high, potassium.

steps.x: **E. Spironolactone.** Spironolactone: step 4 if K+ ≤4.5; watch for hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is reviewed 6 weeks after a myocardial infarction treated with PCI. He also has hypertension, with a BP of 150/92 mmHg. His echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 40%. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor and atorvastatin. He has no asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antihypertensive treatment?
questions.e: In hypertension with heart failure or after MI, a beta-blocker plus an ACE inhibitor treats BP and improves prognosis.

steps.x: Post-MI with reduced EF: drugs that **improve prognosis**.

elim: Does not give the prognostic benefit of beta-blockade and ACEi after MI.
No prognostic benefit after MI.
Not used alone; ACEi and beta-blocker come first.
Verapamil is avoided with reduced LV function.

steps.x: **B. Bisoprolol and ramipril.** Hypertension post-MI or with heart failure: beta-blocker + ACE inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a phaeochromocytoma confirmed by raised plasma free metanephrines and a 4 cm right adrenal mass on CT. Her BP is 174/104 mmHg with episodes of palpitations. She is listed for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management before surgery?
o: Proceed to surgery without drug preparation
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma is treated by adrenalectomy after alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine), with a beta-blocker added only once alpha-blocked to control tachycardia.

steps.x: Surgery is curative, but **alpha before beta** to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

elim: Beta-blockade first leaves alpha effects unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis.
Tumour handling releases catecholamines; she needs alpha-blockade first.
Do not block catecholamine surges.
Treats hyperaldosteronism, not catecholamine excess.

steps.x: **B. Phenoxybenzamine, then a beta-blocker.** Phaeo: alpha-blocker first, then beta-blocker, then adrenalectomy.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has essential hypertension. Investigations show no secondary cause. A student asks which haemodynamic change mainly sustains his raised BP years after diagnosis. His resting pulse rate is 68 bpm and echocardiogram shows a normal cardiac output.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism sustaining his hypertension?
questions.e: Essential hypertension arises from genetics, increased sympathetic activity, RAAS overactivity and environment, and is sustained by a raised peripheral vascular resistance.

steps.x: BP = cardiac output × resistance; output is **normal**, so resistance is up.

elim: Not the main determinant in essential hypertension.
His cardiac output is normal.
Would lower, not raise, BP.
Sympathetic activity is increased in essential hypertension.

steps.x: **C. Increased peripheral vascular resistance.** Established essential hypertension = raised peripheral vascular resistance.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with peripheral arterial disease has hypertension and a 75% stenosis of the left renal artery on angiography. Her plasma renin activity is raised. Her potassium is 3.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypertension?
o: Autonomous aldosterone secretion by the adrenal
Catecholamine release from the adrenal medulla
Excess cortisol acting on mineralocorticoid receptors
Primary sodium loss from the kidney
Reduced renal perfusion activating the renin-angiotensin system
questions.e: Low perfusion pressure beyond the stenosis triggers renin release; angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone causes sodium retention (secondary hyperaldosteronism, hence raised renin and low potassium).

clues: 75% stenosis of the left renal artery
steps.x: Stenosis + **high renin** = renin-driven (secondary) hyperaldosteronism.

elim: That is primary hyperaldosteronism, with suppressed renin.
That is phaeochromocytoma.
That is Cushing's; renin would not be raised.
Would lower BP.

steps.x: **E. Reduced renal perfusion activating the renin-angiotensin system.** RAS: low perfusion → renin → angiotensin II and aldosterone → hypertension.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has hypertension with a potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. He takes no diuretics. Investigations confirm bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia. He starts a drug that blocks the hormonal cause.
questions.q: Which pattern of plasma hormones is most likely before treatment?
questions.e: In primary hyperaldosteronism aldosterone is made independently of the renin-angiotensin system, causing sodium and water retention (hypertension) and renal potassium loss; the volume load suppresses renin. Spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor.

steps.x: Primary (adrenal) source = aldosterone **high**, renin **suppressed**.

elim: Secondary hyperaldosteronism, as in renal artery stenosis.
Seen in Addison's disease (adrenal failure).
Seen with liquorice or Liddle syndrome.
Would not explain hypokalaemic hypertension.

steps.x: **B. High aldosterone with low renin.** Conn's: high aldosterone, low renin; treat bilateral disease with spironolactone.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations. Her plasma free metanephrines are raised and CT shows a 3 cm adrenal mass. Histology after adrenalectomy shows cells that stain brown with chromium salts.
questions.q: From which cells did the tumour most likely arise?
o: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour of medullary chromaffin cells; surges of adrenaline and noradrenaline act on alpha and beta receptors to cause headache, sweating and tachycardia.

steps.x: Catecholamine excess + **chromaffin** staining = adrenal medulla.

elim: Give medullary thyroid carcinoma, which secretes calcitonin.
Produce cortisol (Cushing's adenoma).
Produce aldosterone (Conn's adenoma).
Produce adrenal androgens.

steps.x: **A. Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.** Phaeochromocytoma = chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, acting via alpha/beta receptors.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with hypertension is started on lisinopril. Four weeks later his BP has fallen from 154/96 to 136/84 mmHg and his potassium has risen from 4.2 to 4.9 mmol/L. He has no cough.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the drug lowered his BP?
o: Blockade of aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
Blockade of angiotensin II type 1 receptors
Blockade of L-type calcium channels in arterioles
Inhibition of the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule
Reduced conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
questions.e: ACE inhibitors block ACE, reducing angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (less sodium retention, hence the rise in potassium).

steps.x: An ACE inhibitor; potassium rise = less **aldosterone**.

elim: This is spironolactone's action.
This is how ARBs such as losartan work.
This is how amlodipine works.
This is how thiazide-like diuretics work.

steps.x: **E. Reduced conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.** ACEi: less angiotensin II and aldosterone; side effects hyperkalaemia and (bradykinin) cough.
